At 67, with 45 years behind me and a diploma from the agricultural college that I earned right after the reforms began, I don't need a textbook to tell me what my fields need. But I also know that theory and dirt are two different things. My 16.1 mu is split between 10 mu in the wheat-maize rotation and 6.1 mu in cotton. My wife works part-time at the garment factory in town, so most days it's just me, and my back reminds me of that every evening.

The winter wheat went in last October 12th, a bit earlier than some neighbors because I wanted good tillering before winter. I used an improved semi-dwarf variety, Jinmai 47, at 12.5 kg/mu. For base fertilizer I put down 150 kg/mu of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) plus 5 kg/mu of urea — that gave me about 12 kg N, 7 kg P, and 7 kg K per mu. The wheat overwintered reasonably well, but the spring return has been dry, so I'm planning three irrigations: returning-green water in early March, one at jointing in mid-April, and a final one at grain filling in mid-May if the sky stays clear. Each irrigation runs me about 35 yuan/mu for electricity and water fees. For the spring topdress, I'll apply another 8 kg N/mu as urea at jointing, bringing my total N to 20 kg/mu. I'm targeting 480 kg/mu yield based on the stand count and tiller number I see now. I'll spray a broadleaf herbicide in March and watch for powdery mildew — if I see it, I'll hit it with fungicide at heading.

For cotton, I'm planting the 6.1 mu in plastic mulch around April 22nd with a hybrid Bt cotton, mainly for the bollworm resistance. Seed cost is about 50 yuan/mu. I'll band-apply 80 kg/mu of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) at planting, which gives me about 12 kg N, 6 kg P, and 6 kg K per mu, then side-dress another 4 kg N/mu at flowering in July. Cotton needs careful water management — two irrigations, one at flowering and one at peak boll, about 40 yuan/mu each. I'm budgeting four insecticide sprays: one preventive for aphids, two for bollworm backup (even with Bt), and one for spider mites if the summer turns hot and dry. I expect about 260 kg lint per mu if the weather cooperates, but cotton prices have been volatile, so I'm not counting on it.

The summer maize is the one that always makes me nervous because of the timing. I have the custom combine booked for June 10th — non-negotiable. Immediately after wheat harvest, I'll plant a hybrid maize, Zhengdan 958, at 4.5 kg/mu. That variety has never let me down in 15 years. For fertilizer, I'll apply 15 kg N/mu total, split as 8 kg N at planting (as compound fertilizer) and 7 kg N as urea topdress at the 8-leaf stage around mid-July. Two irrigations: one if June is dry at seedling stage, and one critical one at silking in early August. Maize seed is 45 yuan/mu. I'm expecting 520 kg/mu — last year I got 510, and the soil organic matter on that plot has been climbing slowly.

Labor is my binding constraint. For wheat, I'll handle the spraying and fertilizing myself, but I need 3 days of hired labor at harvest — the window is too tight and I can't afford a delay if rain comes. For maize planting, my nephew will help for 2 days, plus I hire a tractor for tillage and planting. Cotton is the real labor hog: I'll need 10 days of hired labor just for picking in September and October, at 120 yuan per day. My wife can help with cotton picking on weekends, but her factory job is strict.

Total input cash outlay this year — seed, fertilizer, pesticide, irrigation — comes to about 9,200 yuan. That's a big chunk of our liquid savings, but going cheap on fertilizer is a false economy. I've seen what happens when you under-fertilize wheat: the yield drop costs you three times what you saved. Still, I'm not pushing to the theoretical optimum. At my age, stability matters more than squeezing out every last kilogram.
